4918.dq: it seems to be the case that stress assignment in Aro is entirely predictable from a word’s syllable structure ... stress can then be assigned to a word according to the following set of rules (pp. 117, 121); illustrated with isolated words and inflected verb forms, e.g. /fa.lip/ 'dust' (initial), /ɨ.sɨn/ 'again' (final), /key.ga.təy/ 'NON1.SG-put' (4.3.3, penult).
4918.dloc: Section 2.5 'Stress', pp. 117-128: intro p. 117; §2.5.1 correlates pp. 117-118; §2.5.2 weight rules p. 120 and Table 2.29 p. 121; §2.5.3 'Rules for assigning stress' p. 121; worked examples pp. 122-127; Tables 2.30-2.32 pp. 128ff. Table 1.1 p. 10: 'Contrastive stress... no', 'Tone... no'.
4918.heavy: Syllable weight (represented here on a scale from one to four) is assigned according to the following set of rules: A weight of one is assigned to syllables whose nucleus is a monophthong short vowel (/ə/ or /ɨ/) and which do not have a consonant coda. A weight of two is assigned to syllables whose nucleus is a monophthong short vowel (/ə/ or /ɨ/) and which have a consonant coda. A weight of three is assigned to syllables whose nucleus is either a monophthong medium-duration vowel (/a/, /i/, or /u/) or a diphthong consisting of a short vowel (/ə/ or /ɨ/) and a glide. A weight of four is assigned to syllables whose nucleus is either a monophthong long vowel (/e/, /o/, /ā/, or /æ/) or a diphthong consisting of a medium-duration or long vowel (i.e. any vowel other than /ə/ and /ɨ/) and a glide. (§2.5.2, p. 120, p. 143)
4918.dflt: When the last two visible syllables are of equal weight, stress falls on the penultimate visible syllable: /sɨp.sɨp/ 2.2 initial, /kar.kəu/ 3.3 initial, /cay.koy/ 4.4 initial, /ka.rɨ.ram/ 3.1.3 initial (= antepenult, medial weight-1 syllable skipped), /key.ga.təy/ 4.3.3 penult, /ay.mā.ro/ 4.4.4 penult. When only one visible syllable remains it is stressed regardless of position (/ə.dəlp/ 1.2 final, /a.gə/ 3.1 initial). No polysyllabic words of weight-1 syllables only are attested (fn. 39).
4918.prule: Single word stress in a right-edge two-syllable window over a four-degree weight scale (1 = open syllable with short /ə ɨ/; 2 = closed syllable with short /ə ɨ/; 3 = /a i u/ nucleus or short vowel + glide; 4 = long /e o ā æ/ or non-short vowel + glide). The rightmost weight-1 syllable is extrametrical; if only one visible syllable remains it is stressed; otherwise the heavier of the last two visible syllables is stressed, and if they are of equal weight the penultimate visible syllable is stressed (trochaic default). Correlates: greater loudness and higher pitch, not duration.
4918.srule: Not mentioned in Drinfeld 2024, Section 2.5 'Stress', pp. 117-132 (whole section, worked examples and Tables 2.30-2.32 read; full-text search of the dissertation for secondary/rhythmic/alternating stress finds nothing). The rules and all examples mark one stressed syllable per word.

4922.dq: In Tiriyó, there are two main prosodic phenomena: rhythmic stress (with the phonological word as its domain) and intonational contours (with the utterance as their domain). [p. 60]
4922.heavy: Heavy = non-(C)V syllables: (C)Vh, (C)VN, CViVj, CViVjh, CViVjN (types listed pp. 62-63, examples (30a-f)); h and N are the only codas. 'Non-(C)V syllables behave differently: they conserve their stress regardless of their position within the word... the presence of non-(C)V syllables disturbs the alternating stress pattern on following (C)V syllables: the pattern restarts with an unstressed syllable, as if a new word had begun.' [p. 62, scan]
4922.dflt: All-light words: every second syllable from the left, final never stressed (3: 010, 4: 0100, 5: 01010, 6: 010100, 7: 0101010, 8: 01010100, Table 2.7 p. 61); all-light bisyllables and monosyllables get no stress (00, 0), only a pitch drop in isolation.
4922.prule: Iterative iambic rhythmic stress over the phonological word, computed left to right: the final syllable is never stressed; every non-final heavy syllable (non-(C)V: (C)Vh, (C)VN, CViVj, CViVjh, CViVjN) is stressed and restarts the alternation after it; every second light syllable, counting from the word start or from the nearest heavy syllable, is stressed. All-light words: 2nd, 4th, 6th... syllables stressed (apoto [a.pó:.to], kit-apoto-ma-ti [ki.tá:.po.tó:.ma.ti]). No culminative primary stress is identified (p. 71).
4922.srule: No primary/secondary hierarchy: every stress placed by rules (i)-(iii) (each non-final heavy syllable; every second light syllable counted from the word start or from the nearest heavy syllable; never the final syllable) is an equal rhythmic stress, and no single syllable is analysed as bearing primary stress -- 'aside from an impression that the last stressed syllable in a phonological word sounds stronger than the others, there seems to be no reason to analyze any single syllable in a phonological word as bearing primary stress' (Meira 1999: 71).
4922.quote: The following rules summarize the various facts described above, giving an overall characterization of Tiriyó rhythmic stress in terms of (C)V ('light') or non-(C)V ('heavy') syllables. (i) Final syllables are not stressed. (ii) Every non-final heavy syllable is stressed. (iii) Every second light syllable, counting from either the beginning of the word or the nearest heavy syllable, is stressed. [p. 63] ... Tiriyó phonological words follow a pattern of alternation between non-prominent (unstressed) and prominent (stressed) syllables. If the phonological word is composed exclusively of (C)V sy…
4922.idn: Tiriyó (the language of the c. 2,000 Tiriyó on both sides of the Brazil-Surinam border; speakers' autodenomination tarëno; no narrower dialect singled out for the description); data: Author's own fieldwork with consultants in Missão Tiriós and Matawaré (Brazil, upper Paru de Oeste) and in Tepoe and Kuwamarasamutu…
4922.exq_: (i) Final syllables are not stressed. (ii) Every non-final heavy syllable is stressed. (iii) Every second light syllable, counting from either the beginning of the word or the nearest heavy syllable, is stressed. [p. 63, no exceptions stated] ... the iambic stress system would not assign any stress…
4922.tone: Not tonal. 'high pitch, unlike length, is not an automatic element of stress; rather, it is an intonational element, which interacts with the stressed or unstressed status of a syllable... but is not part of it' (§2.5.1.3, pp. 70-71).

4923.prule: Lexical pitch accent, not stress: an H-L pitch drop inside the phonological word is distinctive. Every stem is either unaccented (= default stem-final accent; suffixes are low-pitched) or carries a marked accent that must be lexically indicated and can only sit on the penult of the stem; at most one accent per phonological word; compounds take the accent of their last element; given the accent location the surface pitch pattern is automatic (unaccented word-initial and post-accent syllables low, all other syllables high, falling word-finally). 4924.tone: Dornan p. 61: 'There are at least three tones in the Sesarwa language, the high, middle and low', with minimal triples (hwee x3; |gaa x3). Tone is not marked in his wordlists and the grave/breve marks on the p. 63 example sentence are given no key (p. 62 'The Alphabet' covers vowels, consonants and clicks only). Modern descriptions of Northern Tshwa lects treat the language as tonal with the mora as tone-bearing unit and say nothing about stress: Phiri 2021 (Tjwao PhD, ch. 4; tone explicitly not analysed, fn. 45 p. 49, sec. 8.3), Phiri & Andrason 2022 (sketch, p. 4: each vowel a distinct tone-bearing unit), Fehn & Phiri 2017 (p. 107: lexical tone distinctive in all Northern Tshwa varieties, unmarked), Pratchett 2020 (p. 42: tone unmarked), Andrason, Phiri & Fehn 2023 (onomatopoeia prosody only). A reviewer may reasonably read Dornan's final 'accent' as the pitch/intonation impression of a tone language rather than stress; the code follows the source's wording.

4928.tone: Tswa is a tone language (H vs. toneless; Ugembe 2017, Kisseberth & Ugembe 2025). Neither modern source uses the word 'stress': Kisseberth & Ugembe 2025 p. 3 'The penult vowel in the intonational phrase is lengthened. There is a tonal contrast between whether a vowel has a High tone or not'; Gundane 2021 'a duração na penúltima sílaba é somente fonética nesta língua' and length is 'meramente demarcativo que geralmente ocorre na penúltima sílaba, na última ou ainda na primeira sílaba por razões enfáticas'. Gowlett 2003 (Zone S survey, §3.6) calls it a 'penultimate length-stress feature which signals the end of a phrase or sentence in declarative sentences... not used in interrogative and exclamatory sentences'. So the 1902 word-level penult 'accent' is the same non-contrastive penultimate prominence that modern work places at the intonational-phrase edge in a tone language.

4932.tone: Non-ideophonic lexicon: 'there are no lexical or grammatical tonal contrasts' (p. 76); the only High tone is the predictable one on the first mora of the lengthened phrase-penult, which Downing treats as a correlate of phrasal stress / 'intonational level pitch-accent' (p. 79). 4938.dq: Due to logistical constraints related to travel in Arunachal Pradesh, no time was able to be spent discussing topics such as intonation or sandhi. Instead, I am only able to give a basic overview of the tonemes here.
4938.dloc: van Dam: Section 9.2.4 'Tone Categories', p. 241; toneless-prefix sentence sec. 9.2.4, p. 243; group-level presyllable remark sec. 5.1.3, p. 94; Fig. 7.9 caption, sec. 7.2 Khălak (ch. 7 Southern Rangpang Tangsa), p. 188. Sudhakaran: ch. 1, sec. 1.2.4 'Tutsa Tones', p. 12 (chapter-1 p. 12), Table 1.3.
4938.prule: No word-stress rule stated. Tutsa is described as a lexical tone language: van Dam gives four tonemes on the (monosyllabic) stem syllable (1 mid falling breathy, 2 high level, 3 mid/low falling, 4 checked/short with oral or glottal stop coda); Sudhakaran gives two tones (high vs low) with seven minimal pairs. Sesquisyllabic prefixes (/e0/, /a0/, /ə/) are toneless minor syllables, and for the Tangsa-Nocte group generally 'toneless and unstressed'.

A number of segmental combinations have not been adequately recorded, and nothing has been recorded within carrier sentences. Contours in Tutsa differ considerably from many other Tangsa-Nocte varieties. [...] It is still a four-tone system and the etyma fall under the same category as with other Tangsa-Nocte varieties discussed here.…

4938.tone: Both reachable primaries treat Tutsa as a lexical tone language and say nothing about word stress or accent. van Dam (2023, sec. 9.2): four-tone system on stem syllables, citation forms only, no carrier sentences, intonation and sandhi not studied; the only prominence remarks are group-level, not Tutsa-specific (sec. 5.1.3, p. 94 / p. 112: the presyllable is 'toneless and unstressed'; Fig. 7.9 caption, p. 188 / p. 206, in the Khălak section 7.2 of ch. 7 Southern Rangpang Tangsa: sesquisyllabic prefixes 'are common in Tibeto-Burman and are unstressed and atonal'), i.e. the tone-bearing major syllable is the prominent one and minor syllables are not. The two sources disagree on the tone inventory (4 vs 2), not on stress.

4939.tone: The source describes a two-level lexical tone system (H, L; derived phonetic tones incl. a word-final fall and an extra-high tone in the abbreviations list) plus grammatical tone (high-toned negation prefix lV́-, low-toned focus prefix lV̀-, low-tone subjunctive per Harley 2017: 122). The word 'stress' does not occur in the paper; 'accent' occurs only as 'pitch-accent', the in-situ focus marker (abstract; sect. 2.4 pp. 83-84; fn. 6; conclusion p. 88: 'use of a pitch-accent, has rarely been documented in any tone language'). Fn. 6 (p. 84): day-names such as Kofi vary between LH and HL tone patterns across speakers, and the pitch-accent focus effects apply whatever the tone pattern of the word. No statement that the language has, or lacks, word stress.

4941.dloc: Anthropological Linguistics 8(2): 167 (last paragraph) - 168, in Hale's 'Appendix to XXIX: The Paman Group of the Pama-Nyungan Phylic Family'; the four lects are listed as sample members on p. 163 and described on p. 165 (section 'Awŋtim and Ntʳaʔŋit'); the Awngtim metathesis examples are on pp. 172-173; the only synchronic rule, p. 179, is for Linngithigh
4941.prule: No synchronic word-stress rule is stated for Awngtim or Ntra'ngit. The only stress statement is a subgroup-level diachronic one: in the Northern Paman reflection of Proto-Paman, primary stress (called 'a strictly phonetic feature', i.e. non-phonemic) shifted from the initial to the second syllable of the stem, and the initial consonant was then lost in every Northern Paman lect except Uraði and its sister dialects (so in these four). The modern position is not derivable from the source for this lect: short *V₁ was 'lost in some languages, retained in others, and metathesized in still others', Awngtim being a metathesizing lect (p. 172 'The following examples are from Awŋtim', p. 173), so many modern stems are monosyllabic (e.g. *minʸa > ŋya 'animal', *tʸuma > mwa 'fire', *mulir > lwið 'tooth') and no stress-marked Awngtim/Ntra'ngit forms are given.

Stress, accent and prominence are never mentioned in any reachable source.

4943.tone: Lewis 2024 (first-hand, University of Ibadan fieldwork in all three villages) describes H and L lexical tone with gender-based polarisation on non-initial syllables and defers phrase-level tone behaviour; Idialu 2025 p. 45: 'Ubang's phonological system is characterised by a rich inventory of consonants and vowels, including pervasive nasalisation and tonal distinctions. Tones serve both lexical and grammatical functions, distinguishing meaning at both the word and sentence levels (Iwara, 2017)' (that citation could not be verified); Blench 2001 wordlist columns for Ubang (m.) and (f.) are tone-marked (ò-nè, ɔ̀-ɲìɲǐE, rì-bE^) but its prose says nothing about tone or stress (a full-text search of the 26-page text for stress/accent/tone finds only 'stone'). No source mentions stress or accent; the only 'stress' hit in Lewis 2024 is the idiom 'it should be stressed that' (p. 7).

tn.quote: Yet another attested form of lexical gender manifestation in Ubang is tonal alternation. In certain words, tonal melody polarises across male and female speech. Tonal polarisation is used here in the sense that tones in specific syllables of cognate words consistently differ in female and male versions. This gender-based tonal opposition is usually between low and high tones, such that where the male use high tone, the females substitute with a low tone and vice versa (Table 7). Tonal polarisation is replete after the first syllable of words and has not been found in monosyllabic words.
